entries.519aaccc3febe17fc0a55ba22740d9c3dcc12c44: <div sID="gen9281" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Job.4" sID="Job.4"/> <div eID="gen9281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9282" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9283" type="x-p"/> Job having warmly given vent to his passion, and so broken the ice, his friends here come gravely to give vent to their judgment upon his case, which perhaps they had communicated to one another apart, compared notes upon it and talked it over among themselves, and found they were all agreed in their verdict, that Job's afflictions certainly proved him to be a hypocrite; but they did not attack Job with this high charge till by the expressions of his discontent and impatience, in which they thought he reflected on God himself, he had confirmed them in the bad opinion they had before conceived of him and his character. Now they set upon him with great fear. The dispute begins, and it soon becomes fierce. The opponents are Job's three friends. Job himself is respondent. Elihu appears, first, as moderator, and at length God himself gives judgment upon the controversy and the management of it. The question in dispute is whether Job was an honest man or no, the same question that was in dispute between God and Satan in the first two chapters. Satan had yielded it, and durst not pretend that his cursing his day was a constructive cursing of his God; no, he cannot deny but that Job still holds fast his integrity; but Job's friends will needs have it that, if Job were an honest man, he would not have been thus sorely and thus tediously afflicted, and therefore urge him to confess himself a hypocrite in the profession he had made of religion: "No," says Job, "that I will never do; I have offended God, but my heart, notwithstanding, has been upright with him;" and still he holds fast the comfort of his integrity. Eliphaz, who, it is likely, was the senior, or of the best quality, begins with him in this chapter, in which, I. He bespeaks a patient hearing, <reference osisRef="Job.4.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. He compliments Job with an acknowledgment of the eminence and usefulness of the profession he had made of religion, <reference osisRef="Job.4.3-Job.4.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. He charges him with hypocrisy in his profession, grounding his charge upon his present troubles and his conduct under them, <reference osisRef="Job.4.5-Job.4.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. IV. To make good the inference, he maintains that man's wickedness is that which always brings God's judgments, <reference osisRef="Job.4.7-Job.4.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. V. He corroborates his assertion by a vision which he had, in which he was reminded of the incontestable purity and justice of God, and the meanness, weakness, and sinfulness of man, <reference osisRef="Job.4.12-Job.4.21">ver. 12-21</reference>. By all this he aims to bring down Job's spirit and to make him both penitent and patient under his afflictions.
entries.98986ea13b101c31dc3746e33ab0da58aeee34e9: <div eID="gen9283" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9282" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9284" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said, 2 <hi type="italic">If</hi> we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking? <hi type="super">3</hi> Behold, thou hast instructed many, and thou hast strengthened the weak hands. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees. <hi type="super">5</hi> But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled. <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not <hi type="italic">this</hi> thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways? <div eID="gen9284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9285" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen9285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9286" type="x-p"/> I. Eliphaz excuses the trouble he is now about to give to Job by his discourse (<reference osisRef="Job.4.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If we assay a word with thee,</hi> offer a word of reproof and counsel, wilt thou be grieved and take it ill?" We have reason to fear thou wilt; but there is no remedy: "<hi type="italic">Who can refrain from words?</hi>" Observe, 1. With what modesty he speaks of himself and his own attempt. He will not undertake the management of the cause alone, but very humbly joins his friends with him: "We will commune with thee." Those that plead God's cause must be glad of help, lest it suffer through their weakness. He will not promise much, but begs leave to assay or attempt, and try if he could propose any thing that might be pertinent, and suit Job's case. In difficult matters it becomes us to pretend no further, but only to try what may be said or done. Many excellent discourses have gone under the modest title of <hi type="italic">Essays.</hi> 2. With what tenderness he speaks of Job, and his present afflicted condition: "If we tell thee our mind, <hi type="italic">wilt thou be grieved?</hi> Wilt thou take it ill? Wilt thou lay it to thy own heart as thy affliction or to our charge as our fault? Shall we be reckoned unkind and cruel if we deal plainly and faithfully with thee? We desire we may not; we hope we shall not, and should be sorry if that should be ill resented which is well intended." Note, We ought to be afraid of grieving any, especially those that are already in grief, lest we add affliction to the afflicted, as David's enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>. We should show ourselves backward to say that which we foresee will be grievous, though ever so necessary. God himself, though he afflicts justly, does not afflict willingly, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.33">Lam. iii. 33</reference>. 3. With what assurance he speaks of the truth and pertinency of what he was about to say: <hi type="italic">Who can withhold himself from speaking?</hi> Surely it was a pious zeal for God's honour, and the spiritual welfare of Job, that laid him under this necessity of speaking. "Who can forbear speaking in vindication of God's honour, which we hear reproved, in love to thy soul, which we see endangered?" Note, It is foolish pity not to reprove our friends, even our friends in affliction, for what they say or do amiss, only for fear of offending them. Whether men take it well or ill, we must with wisdom and meekness do our duty and discharge a good conscience. <div eID="gen9286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9287" type="x-p"/> II. He exhibits a twofold charge against Job. <div eID="gen9287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9288" type="x-p"/> 1. As to his particular conduct under this affliction. He charges him with weakness and faint-heartedness, and this article of his charge there was too much ground for, <reference osisRef="Job.4.3-Job.4.5">v. 3-5</reference>. And here, <div eID="gen9288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9289" type="x-p"/> (1.) He takes notice of Job's former serviceableness to the comfort of others. He owns that Job had instructed many, not only his own children and servants, but many others, his neighbours and friends, as many as fell within the sphere of his activity. He did not only encourage those who were teachers by office, and countenance them, and pay for the teaching of those who were poor, but he did himself instruct many. Though a great man, he did not think it below him (king Solomon was a preacher); though a man of business, he found time to do it, went among his neighbours, talked to them about their souls, and gave them good counsel. O that this example of Job were imitated by our great men! If he met with those who were ready to fall into sin, or sink under their troubles, his words upheld them: a wonderful dexterity he had in offering that which was proper to fortify persons against temptations, to support them under their burdens, and to comfort afflicted consciences. He had, and used, the tongue of the learned, knew how to speak a word in season to those that were weary, and employed himself much in that good work. With suitable counsels and comforts he <hi type="italic">strengthened the weak hands</hi> for work and service and the spiritual warfare, and the feeble knees for bearing up the man in his journey and under his load. It is not only our duty to <hi type="italic">lift up our own hands that hang down,</hi> by quickening and encouraging ourselves in the way of duty (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.12">Heb. xii. 12</reference>), but we must also strengthen the weak hands of others, as there is occasion, and do what we can to confirm their feeble knees, by saying <hi type="italic">to those that are of a fearful heart, Be strong,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.35.3-Isa.35.4">Isa. xxxv. 3, 4</reference>. The expressions seem to be borrowed thence. Note, Those should abound in spiritual charity. A good word, well and wisely spoken, may do more good than perhaps we think of. But why does Eliphaz mention this here? [1.] Perhaps he praises him thus for the good he had done that he might make the intended reproof the more passable with him. Just commendation is a good preface to a just reprehension, will help to remove prejudices, and will show that the reproof comes not from ill will. Paul praised the Corinthians before he chided them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.2">1 Cor. xi. 2</reference>. [2.] He remembers how Job had comforted others as a reason why he might justly expect to be himself comforted; and yet, if conviction was necessary in order to comfort, they must be excused if they applied themselves to that first. The <hi type="italic">Comforter shall reprove,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.8">John xvi. 8</reference>. [3.] He speaks this, perhaps, in a way of pity, lamenting that through the extremity of his affliction he could not apply those comforts to himself which he had formerly administered to others. It is easier to give good counsel than to take it, to preach meekness and patience than to practise them. <hi type="italic">Facile omnes, cum valemus, rectum consilium ægrotis damus—We all find it easy, when in health, to give good advice to the sick.—Terent.</hi> [4.] Most think that he mentions it as an aggravation of his present discontent, upbraiding him with his knowledge, and the good offices he had done for others, as if he had said, "Thou that hast taught others, why dost thou not teach thyself? Is not this an evidence of thy hypocrisy, that thou hast prescribed that medicine to others which thou wilt not now take thyself, and so contradictest thyself, and actest against thy own known principles? Thou that teachest another to faint, dost thou faint? <reference osisRef="Rom.2.21">Rom. ii. 21</reference>. Physician, heal thyself." Those who have rebuked others must expect to hear of it if they themselves become obnoxious to rebuke. <div eID="gen9289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9290" type="x-p"/> (2.) He upbraids him with his present low-spiritedness, <reference osisRef="Job.4.5">v. 5</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Now</hi> that <hi type="italic">it has come upon thee,</hi> now that it is thy turn to be afflicted, and the bitter cup that goes round is put into thy hand, now that <hi type="italic">it touches thee, thou faintest, thou art troubled.</hi>" Here, [1.] He makes too light of Job's afflictions: "It <hi type="italic">touches</hi> thee." The very word that Satan himself had used, <reference osisRef="Job.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.2.5">ii. 5</reference>. Had Eliphaz felt but the one-half of Job's affliction, he would have said, "It smites me, it wounds me;" but, speaking of Job's afflictions, he makes a mere trifle of it: "It touches thee and thou canst not bear to be touched." <hi type="italic">Noli me tangere—Touch me not.</hi> [2.] He makes too much of Job's resentments, and aggravates them: "Thou faintest, or thou art beside thyself; thou ravest, and knowest not what thou sayest." Men in deep distress must have grains of allowance, and a favourable construction put upon what they say; when we make the worst of every word we do not as we would be done by. <div eID="gen9290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9291" type="x-p"/> 2. As to his general character before this affliction. He charges him with wickedness and false-heartedness, and this article of his charge was utterly groundless and unjust. How unkindly does he banter him, and upbraid him with the great profession of religion he had made, as if it had all now come to nothing and proved a sham (<reference osisRef="Job.4.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways?</hi> Does it not all appear now to be a mere pretence? For, hadst thou been sincere in it, God would not thus have afflicted thee, nor wouldst thou have behaved thus under the affliction." This was the very thing Satan aimed at, to prove Job a hypocrite, and disprove the character God had given of him. When he could not himself do this to God, but he still saw and said, <hi type="italic">Job is perfect and upright,</hi> then he endeavoured, by his friends, to do it to Job himself, and to persuade him to confess himself a hypocrite. Could he have gained that point he would have triumphed. <hi type="italic">Habes confitentem reum—Out of thy own mouth will I condemn thee.</hi> But, by the grace of God, Job was enabled to hold fast his integrity, and would not bear false witness against himself. Note, Those that pass rash and uncharitable censures upon their brethren, and condemn them as hypocrites, do Satan's work, and serve his interest, more than they are aware of. I know not how it comes to pass that <reference osisRef="Job.4.6">this verse</reference> is differently read in several editions of our common English Bibles; the original, and all the ancient versions, put <hi type="italic">thy hope</hi> before <hi type="italic">the uprightness of thy ways.</hi> So does the Geneva, and most of the editions of the last translation; but I find one of the first, in 1612, has it, <hi type="italic">Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, the uprightness of thy ways, and thy hope?</hi> Both the Assembly's Annotations and Mr. Pool's have that reading: and an edition in 1660 reads it, "<hi type="italic">Is not thy fear thy confidence, and the uprightness of thy ways thy hope?</hi> Does it not appear now that all the religion both of thy devotion and of thy conversation was only in hope and confidence that thou shouldst grow rich by it? Was it not all mercenary?" The very thing that Satan suggested. <hi type="italic">Is not thy religion thy hope, and are not thy ways thy confidence?</hi> so Mr. Broughton. Or, "Was it not? Didst thou not think that that would be thy protection? But thou art deceived." Or, "Would it not have been so? If it had been sincere, would it not have kept thee from this despair?" It is true, <hi type="italic">if thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength,</hi> thy grace, <hi type="italic">is small</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.10">Prov. xxiv. 10</reference>); but it does not therefore follow that thou hast no grace, no strength at all. A man's character is not to be taken from a single act.
entries.bb0e758e4ded24c88174be305bc14f5e02d62e6c: <div eID="gen9291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9292" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Remember, I pray thee, who <hi type="italic">ever</hi> perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off? 8 Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. <hi type="super">9</hi> By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed. <hi type="super">10</hi> The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. <hi type="super">11</hi> The old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad. <div eID="gen9292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9293" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz here advances another argument to prove Job a hypocrite, and will have not only his impatience under his afflictions to be evidence against him but even his afflictions themselves, being so very great and extraordinary, and there being no prospect at all of his deliverance out of them. To strengthen his argument he here lays down these two principles, which seem plausible enough:— <div eID="gen9293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9294" type="x-p"/> I. That good men were never thus ruined. For the proof of this he appeals to Job's own observation (<reference osisRef="Job.4.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Remember, I pray thee;</hi> recollect all that thou hast seen, heard, or read, and give me an instance of any one that was innocent and righteous, and yet perished as thou dost, and was cut off as thou art." If we understand it of a final and eternal destruction, his principle is true. None that are innocent and righteous perish for ever: it is only a <hi type="italic">man of sin</hi> that is a <hi type="italic">son of perdition,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2 Thess. ii. 3</reference>. But then it is ill applied to Job; he did not thus perish, nor was he cut off: a man is never undone till he is in hell. But, if we understand it of any temporal calamity, his principle is not true. <hi type="italic">The righteous perish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa. lvii. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">there is one event both to the righteous and to the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Eccl. ix. 2</reference>), both in life and death; the great and certain difference is after death. Even before Job's time (as early as it was) there were instances sufficient to contradict this principle. Did not righteous Abel <hi type="italic">perish being innocent?</hi> and was he not cut off in the beginning of his days? Was not righteous Lot burnt out of house and harbour, and forced to retire to a melancholy cave? Was not righteous Jacob <hi type="italic">a Syrian ready to perish?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deut. xxvi. 5</reference>. Other such instances, no doubt, there were, which are not on record. <div eID="gen9294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9295" type="x-p"/> II. That wicked men were often thus ruined. For the proof of this he vouches his own observation (<reference osisRef="Job.4.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Even as I have seen,</hi> many a time, <hi type="italic">those that plough iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap accordingly; by the blast of God they perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.4.9">v. 9</reference>. We have daily instances of that; and therefore, since thou dost thus perish and art consumed, we have reason to think that, whatever profession of religion thou hast made, thou hast but ploughed iniquity and sown wickedness. Even as I have seen in others, so do I see in thee." <div eID="gen9295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9296" type="x-p"/> 1. He speaks of sinners in general, politic busy sinners, that take pains in sin, for they plough iniquity; and expect gain by sin, for they sow wickedness. Those that plough plough in hope, but what is the issue? <hi type="italic">They reap the same.</hi> They shall of the <hi type="italic">flesh reap corruption</hi> and ruin, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8">Gal. vi. 7, 8</reference>. The harvest will be <hi type="italic">a heap in the day of grief and desperate sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.17.11">Isa. xvii. 11</reference>. He shall reap <hi type="italic">the same,</hi> that is, the proper product of that seedness. That which the sinner sows, he <hi type="italic">sows not that body that shall be,</hi> but God will give it a body, a body of death, <hi type="italic">the end of those things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Rom. vi. 21</reference>. Some, by iniquity and wickedness, understand wrong and injury done to others. Those who plough and sow them shall reap the same, that is, they shall be paid in their own coin. Those who are troublesome shall be troubled, <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6">2 Thess. i. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.25">Josh. vii. 25</reference>. The <hi type="italic">spoilers shall be spoiled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>), and those that led captive shall <hi type="italic">go captive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. He further describes their destruction (<reference osisRef="Job.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">By the blast of God they perish.</hi> The projects they take so much pains in are defeated; God cuts asunder the cords of those ploughers, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3-Ps.129.4">Ps. cxxix. 3, 4</reference>. They themselves are destroyed, which is the just punishment of their iniquity. <hi type="italic">They perish,</hi> that is, they are destroyed utterly; <hi type="italic">they are consumed,</hi> that is, they are destroyed gradually; and this by the blast and breath of God, that is, (1.) By his wrath. His anger is the ruin of sinners, who are therefore called <hi type="italic">vessels of wrath,</hi> and his breath is said to <hi type="italic">kindle Tophet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of his anger?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Ps. xc. 11</reference>. (2.) By his word. He speaks and it is done, easily and effectually. The Spirit of God, in the word, consumes sinners; with that he slays them, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.5">Hos. vi. 5</reference>. Saying and doing are not two things with God. The man of sin is said to be consumed with the <hi type="italic">breath of Christ's mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8 Isa.11.4">2 Thess. ii. 8. Compare Isa. xi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.21">Rev. xix. 21</reference>. Some think that in attributing the destruction of sinners to the blast of God, and <hi type="italic">the breath of his nostrils,</hi> he refers to the wind which blew the house down upon Job's children, as if they were therefore <hi type="italic">sinners above all men because they suffered such things.</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.13.2">Luke xiii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen9296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9297" type="x-p"/> 2. He speaks particularly of tyrants and cruel oppressors, under the similitude of lions, <reference osisRef="Job.4.10-Job.4.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Observe, (1.) How he describes their cruelty and oppression. The Hebrew tongue has five several names for lions, and they are all here used to set forth the terrible tearing power, fierceness, and cruelty, of proud oppressors. They roar, and rend, and prey upon all about them, and bring up their young ones to do so too, <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.3">Ezek. xix. 3</reference>. The devil is a roaring lion; and they partake of his nature, and do his lusts. They are strong as lions, and subtle (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">Ps. x. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.12">xvii. 12</reference>); and, as far as they prevail, they lay all desolate about them. (2.) How he describes their destruction, the destruction both of their power and of their persons. They shall be restrained from doing further hurt and reckoned with for the hurt they have done. An effectual course shall be taken, [1.] That they shall not terrify. The voice of their roaring shall be stopped. [2.] That they shall not tear. God will disarm them, will take away their power to do hurt: <hi type="italic">The teeth of the young lions are broken.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Ps. iii. 7</reference>. Thus shall the remainder of wrath be restrained. [3.] That they shall not enrich themselves with the spoil of their neighbours. Even <hi type="italic">the old lion</hi> is famished, and <hi type="italic">perishes for lack of prey.</hi> Those that have surfeited on spoil and rapine are perhaps reduced to such straits as to die of hunger at last. [4.] That they shall not, as they promise themselves, leave a succession: <hi type="italic">The stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad,</hi> to seek for food themselves, which the old ones used to bring in for them, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.12">Nah. ii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">The lion did tear in pieces for his whelps,</hi> but now they must shift for themselves. Perhaps Eliphaz intended, in this, to reflect upon Job, as if he, being the <hi type="italic">greatest of all the men of the east,</hi> had got his estate by spoil and used his power in oppressing his neighbours, but now his power and estate were gone, and his family was scattered: if so, it was a pity that a man whom God praised should be thus abused.
entries.ac265c9efd5ab3468edcc60c8336477a3f3d662f: <div eID="gen9297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9298" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Now a thing was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a little thereof. <hi type="super">13</hi> In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men, <hi type="super">14</hi> Fear came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones to shake. 15 Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up: <hi type="super">16</hi> It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof: an image <hi type="italic">was</hi> before mine eyes, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> silence, and I heard a voice, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? <hi type="super">18</hi> Behold, he put no trust in his servants; and his angels he charged with folly: <hi type="super">19</hi> How much less <hi type="italic">in</hi> them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the dust, <hi type="italic">which</hi> are crushed before the moth? 20 They are destroyed from morning to evening: they perish for ever without any regarding <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">21</hi> Doth not their excellency <hi type="italic">which is</hi> in them go away? they die, even without wisdom. <div eID="gen9298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9299" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, having undertaken to convince Job of the sin and folly of his discontent and impatience, here vouches a vision he had been favoured with, which he relates to Job for his conviction. What comes immediately from God all men will pay a particular deference to, and Job, no doubt, as much as any. Some think Eliphaz had this vision now <hi type="italic">lately,</hi> since he came to Job, putting words into his mouth wherewith to reason with him; and it would have been well if he had kept to the purport of this vision, which would serve for a ground on which to reprove Job for his murmuring, but not to condemn him as a hypocrite. Others think he had it <hi type="italic">formerly;</hi> for God did, in this way, often communicate his mind to the children of men in those first ages of the world, <reference osisRef="Job.33.15">ch. xxxiii. 15</reference>. Probably God had sent Eliphaz this messenger and message some time or other, when he was himself in an unquiet discontented frame, to calm and pacify him. Note, As we should comfort others with that wherewith we have been comforted (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4">2 Cor. i. 4</reference>), so we should endeavour to convince others with that which has been powerful to convince us. The people of God had not then any written word to quote, and therefore God sometimes notified to them even common truths by the extraordinary ways of revelation. We that have Bibles have there (thanks be to God) a more sure word to depend upon than even visions and voices, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2 Pet. i. 19</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen9299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9300" type="x-p"/> I. The manner in which this message was sent to Eliphaz, and the circumstances of the conveyance of it to him. 1. It was <hi type="italic">brought to him secretly,</hi> or by stealth. Some of the sweetest communion gracious souls have with God is in secret, where no eye sees but that of him who is all eye. God has ways of bringing conviction, counsel, and comfort, to his people, unobserved by the world, by private whispers, as powerfully and effectually as by the public ministry. <hi type="italic">His secret is with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>. As the evil spirit often steals good words out of the heart (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.19">Matt. xiii. 19</reference>), so the good Spirit sometimes steals good words into the heart, or ever we are aware. 2. <hi type="italic">He received a little thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.4.12">v. 12</reference>. And it is but a little of divine knowledge that the best receive in this world. We know little in comparison with what is to be known, and with what we shall know when we come to heaven. <hi type="italic">How little a portion is heard of God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">ch. xxvi. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">We know but in part,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1 Cor. xiii. 12</reference>. See his humility and modesty. He pretends not to have understood it fully, but something of it he perceived. 3. It was brought to him in the <hi type="italic">visions of the night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.13">v. 13</reference>), when he had retired from the world and the hurry of it, and all about him was composed and quiet. Note, The more we are withdrawn from the world and the things of it the fitter we are for communion with God. When we are <hi type="italic">communing with our own hearts, and are still</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Ps. iv. 4</reference>), then is a proper time for the Holy Spirit to commune with us. When others were asleep Eliphaz was ready to receive this visit from Heaven, and probably, like David, was <hi type="italic">meditating upon God in the night-watches;</hi> in the midst of those good thoughts this thing was brought to him. We should hear more from God if we thought more of him; yet some are surprised with convictions in the night, <reference osisRef="Job.33.14-Job.33.15">ch. xxxiii. 14, 15</reference>. 4. It was prefaced with terrors: <hi type="italic">Fear came upon him, and trembling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.4.14">v. 14</reference>. It should seem, before he either heard or saw any thing, he was seized with this trembling, which shook his bones, and perhaps the bed under him. A holy awe and reverence of God and his majesty being struck upon his spirit, he was thereby prepared for a divine visit. Whom God intends to honour he first humbles and lays low, and will have us all to serve him with holy fear, and to rejoice with trembling. <div eID="gen9300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9301" type="x-p"/> II. The messenger by whom it was sent—<hi type="italic">a spirit,</hi> one of the good angels, who are employed not only as the ministers of God's providence, but sometimes as the ministers of his word. Concerning this apparition which Eliphaz saw we are here told (<reference osisRef="Job.4.15-Job.4.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), 1. That it was real, and not a dream, not a fancy. <hi type="italic">An image</hi> was before his eyes; he plainly saw it; at first it passed and repassed before his face, moved up and down, but at length it <hi type="italic">stood still</hi> to speak to him. If some have been so knavish as to impose false visions on others, and some so foolish as to be themselves imposed upon, it does not therefore follow but that there may have been apparitions of spirits, both good and bad. 2. That it was indistinct, and somewhat confused. He <hi type="italic">could not discern the form thereof,</hi> so as to frame any exact idea of it in his own mind, much less to give a description of it. His conscience was to be awakened and informed, not his curiosity gratified. We know little of spirits; we are not capable of knowing much of them, nor is it fit that we should: all in good time; we must shortly remove to the world of spirits, and shall then be better acquainted with them. 3. That it puts him into a great consternation, so that his hair stood on end. Ever since man sinned it has been terrible to him to receive an express from heaven, as conscious to himself that he can expect no good tidings thence; apparitions therefore, even of good spirits, have always made deep impressions of fear, even upon good men. How well it is for us that God sends us his messages, not by spirits, but by men like ourselves, <hi type="italic">whose terror shall not make us afraid!</hi> See <reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">Dan. vii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.8-Dan.10.9">x. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen9301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9302" type="x-p"/> III. The message itself. Before it was delivered <hi type="italic">there was silence,</hi> profound silence, <reference osisRef="Job.4.16">v. 16</reference>. When we are to speak either from God or to him it becomes us to address ourselves to it with a solemn pause, and so to set bounds about the mount on which God is to come down, and not be hasty to utter any thing. It was in a still small voice that the message was delivered, and this was it (<reference osisRef="Job.4.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Shall mortal man be more just than God,</hi> the immortal God? <hi type="italic">Shall a man be</hi> thought to be, or pretend to be, <hi type="italic">more pure than his Maker?</hi> Away with such a thought!" 1. Some think that Eliphaz aims hereby to prove that Job's great afflictions were a certain evidence of his being a wicked man. A mortal man would be thought unjust and very impure if he should thus correct and punish a servant or subject, unless he had been guilty of some very great crime: "If therefore there were not some great crimes for which God thus punishes thee, man would be more just than God, which is not to be imagined." 2. I rather think it is only a reproof of Job's murmuring and discontent: "Shall a man pretend to be more just and pure than God? more truly to understand, and more strictly to observe, the rules and laws of equity than God? Shall <hi type="italic">Enosh,</hi> mortal and miserable man, be so insolent; nay, shall <hi type="italic">Geber,</hi> the strongest and most eminent man, man at his best estate, pretend to compare with God, or stand in competition with him?" Note, It is most impious and absurd to think either others or ourselves more just and pure than God. Those that quarrel and find fault with the directions of the divine law, the dispensations of the divine grace, or the disposals of the divine providence, make themselves more just and pure than God; and those who thus <hi type="italic">reprove God, let them answer it.</hi> What! sinful man! (for he would not have been mortal if he had not been sinful) short-sighted man! Shall he pretend to be more just, more pure, than God, who, being his Maker, is his Lord and owner? Shall the clay contend with the potter? What justice and purity there is in man, God is the author of it, and therefore is himself more just and pure. See <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9-Ps.94.10">Ps. xciv. 9, 10</reference>. <div eID="gen9302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9303" type="x-p"/> IV. The comment which Eliphaz makes upon this, for so it seems to be; yet some take all the <reference osisRef="Job.4.18-Job.4.21">following verses</reference> to be spoken in vision. It comes all to one. <div eID="gen9303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9304" type="x-p"/> 1. He shows how little the angels themselves are in comparison with God, <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">v. 18</reference>. Angels are God's servants, waiting servants, working servants; they are his ministers (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.4">Ps. civ. 4</reference>); bright and blessed beings they are, but God neither needs them nor is benefited by them and is himself infinitely above them, and therefore, (1.) He puts no trust in them, did not repose a confidence in them, as we do in those we cannot live without. There is no service in which he employs them but, if he pleased, he could have it done as well without them. He never made them his confidants, or of his cabinet-council, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">Matt. xxiv. 36</reference>. He does not leave his business wholly to them, but <hi type="italic">his own eyes run to and fro through the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>. See this phrase, <reference osisRef="Job.39.11">ch. xxxix. 11</reference>. Some give this sense of it: "So mutable is even the angelical nature that God would not trust angels with their own integrity; if he had, they would all have done as some did, left their first estate; but he saw it necessary to give them supernatural grace to confirm them." (2.) He charges them with folly, vanity, weakness, infirmity, and imperfection, in comparison with himself. If the world were left to the government of the angels, and they were trusted with the sole management of affairs, they would take false steps, and everything would not be done for the best, as now it is. Angels are intelligences, but finite ones. Though not chargeable with iniquity, yet with imprudence. This last clause is variously rendered by the critics. I think it would bear this reading, repeating the negation, which is very common: <hi type="italic">He will put no trust in his saints; nor will he glory in his angels (in angelis suis non ponet gloriationem) or make his boast</hi> of them, as if their praises, or services, added any thing to him: it is his glory that he is infinitely happy without them. <div eID="gen9304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9305" type="x-p"/> 2. Thence he infers how much less man is, how much less to be trusted in or gloried in. If there is such a distance between God and angels, what is there between God and man! See how man is represented here in his meanness. <div eID="gen9305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9306" type="x-p"/> (1.) Look upon man in his life, and he is very mean, <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">v. 19</reference>. Take man in his best estate, and he is a very despicable creature in comparison with the holy angels, though honourable if compared with the brutes. It is true, angels are spirits, and the souls of men are spirits; but, [1.] Angels are pure spirits; the souls of men <hi type="italic">dwell in houses of clay:</hi> such the bodies of men are. Angels are free; human souls are housed, and the body is a cloud, a clog, to it; it is its cage; it is its prison. It is a house of clay, mean and mouldering; an earthen vessel, soon broken, as it was first formed, according to the good pleasure of the potter. It is a cottage, not a house of cedar or a house of ivory, but of clay, which would soon be in ruins if not kept in constant repair. [2.] Angels are fixed, but the very <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> of that house of clay in which man dwells <hi type="italic">is in the dust.</hi> A house of clay, if built upon a rock, might stand long; but, if founded in the dust, the uncertainty of the foundation will hasten its fall, and it will sink with its own weight. As man was made out of the earth, so he is maintained and supported by that which cometh out of the earth. Take away that, and his body returns to its earth. We stand but upon the dust; some have a higher heap of dust to stand upon than others, but still it is the earth that stays us up and will shortly swallow us up. [3.] Angels are immortal, but man is soon crushed; the <hi type="italic">earthly house of his tabernacle is dissolved;</hi> he <hi type="italic">dies and wastes away, is crushed like a moth</hi> between one's fingers, as easily, as quickly; one may almost as soon kill a man as kill a moth. A little thing will destroy his life. He is <hi type="italic">crushed before the face of the moth,</hi> so the word is. If some lingering distemper, which consumes like a moth, be commissioned to destroy him, he can no more resist it than he can resist an acute distemper, which comes roaring upon him like a lion. See <reference osisRef="Hos.5.12-Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 12-14</reference>. Is such a creature as this to be trusted in, or can any service be expected from him by that God who puts no trust in angels themselves? <div eID="gen9306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9307" type="x-p"/> (2.) Look upon him in his death, and he appears yet more despicable, and unfit to be trusted. Men are mortal and dying, <reference osisRef="Job.4.20-Job.4.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. [1.] In death <hi type="italic">they are destroyed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">perish for ever,</hi> as to this world; it is the final period of their lives, and all the employments and enjoyments here; their place will know them no more. [2.] They are dying daily, and continually wasting: <hi type="italic">Destroyed from morning to evening.</hi> Death is still working in us, like a mole digging our grave at each remove, and we so continually lie exposed that we are killed all the day long. [3.] Their life is short, and in a little time they are cut off. It lasts perhaps but from morning to evening. It is but a day (so some understand it); their birth and death are but the sun-rise and sun-set of the same day. [4.] In death all their excellency passes away; beauty, strength, learning, not only cannot secure them from death, but must die with them, nor shall their pomp, their wealth, or power, descend after them. [5.] Their wisdom cannot save them from death: <hi type="italic">They die without wisdom,</hi> die for want of wisdom, by their own foolish management of themselves, digging their graves with their own teeth. [6.] It is so common a thing that nobody heeds it, nor takes any notice of it: <hi type="italic">They perish without any regarding it,</hi> or laying it to heart. The deaths of others are much the subject of common talk, but little the subject of serious thought. Some think the eternal damnation of sinners is here spoken of, as well as their temporal death: <hi type="italic">They are destroyed, or broken to pieces, by death, from morning to evening; and, if they repent not, they perish for ever</hi> (so some read it), <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">v. 20</reference>. They perish for ever because they regard not God and their duty; they <hi type="italic">consider not their latter end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.1.9">Lam. i. 9</reference>. They have no excellency but that which death takes away, and they die, they die the second death, for want of wisdom to lay hold on eternal life. Shall such a mean, weak, foolish, sinful, dying creature as this pretend to be <hi type="italic">more just than God and more pure than his Maker?</hi> No, instead of quarrelling with his afflictions, let him wonder that he is out of hell.  <chapter eID="Job.4"/> <div eID="gen9307" type="x-p"/>

entries.700e4495931df9dd02e13c2dc78130179e53f5b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4513"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.4.1-Job.4.21">Job 4:1-21</reference>. First Speech of Eliphaz.</title> <div sID="gen6537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4513"/><hi type="bold">1. Eliphaz--</hi>the mildest of Job's three accusers. The greatness of Job's calamities, his complaints against God, and the opinion that calamities are proofs of guilt, led the three to doubt Job's integrity. <div eID="gen6537" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf456302d1b68a8ede9de3290145799491745892: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4514"/><div sID="gen6538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4514"/><hi type="bold">2. If we assay to commune--</hi>Rather, two questions, "May we attempt a word with thee? Wilt thou be grieved at it?" Even pious friends often count that only a touch which we feel as a wound. <div eID="gen6538" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed3c62bd2559093f038ebc3325512490accf4a73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4515"/><div sID="gen6539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4515"/><hi type="bold">3. weak hands--</hi><reference osisRef="Isa.35.3">Is 35:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1">2Sa 4:1</reference>. <div eID="gen6539" type="x-p"/>
entries.21112cc27f4f75317783236555693de584b983ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4516"/><div sID="gen6540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4516"/><hi type="bold">5. thou art troubled--</hi>rather, "unhinged," hast lost thy self-command (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1Th 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen6540" type="x-p"/>
entries.1779fa0fb9bdc01e9aadfcfbe8ac7a0bef3f393e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4517"/><div sID="gen6541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4517"/><hi type="bold">6. Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, &c.--</hi>Does thy fear, thy confidence, come to nothing? Does it come only to this, that thou faintest now? Rather, by transposition, "Is not thy fear (of God) thy hope? and the uprightness of thy ways thy confidence? If so, bethink thee, who ever perished being innocent?" [Umbreit]. But <reference osisRef="Luke.13.2">Lu 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.3">3</reference> shows that, though there is a retributive divine government even in this life, yet we cannot judge by the mere outward appearance. "One event is outwardly to the righteous and to the wicked" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Ec 9:2</reference>); but yet we must take it on trust, that God deals righteously even now (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Psa 37:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Is 33:16</reference>). Judge not by a part, but by the whole of a godly man's life, and by his end, even here (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.11">Jas 5:11</reference>). The one and the same outward event is altogether a different thing in its inward bearings on the godly and on the ungodly even here. Even prosperity, much more calamity, is a punishment to the wicked (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Pr 1:32</reference>). Trials are chastisements for their good (to the righteous) (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.67">Psa 119:67</reference>, 71, 75). See Preface on the Design of this book (see Introduction). <div eID="gen6541" type="x-p"/>
entries.93ca3d19da4536c73ee6ace56183624f8694dca5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4518"/><div sID="gen6542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4518"/><hi type="bold">8. they that plough iniquity ... reap the same--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pr 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Ho 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.13">10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen6542" type="x-p"/>
entries.f77c31e08d9bae5c4798901865c8e940529cc72a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4519"/><div sID="gen6543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4519"/><hi type="bold">9. breath of his nostrils--</hi>God's anger; a figure from the fiery winds of the East (<reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Is 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">Psa 18:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen6543" type="x-p"/>
entries.98ec5a9159f92a771042dc352556630a56c27bf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4520"/><div sID="gen6544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4520"/><hi type="bold">10-11. lion--</hi>that is, wicked men, upon whom Eliphaz wished to show that calamities come in spite of their various resources, just as destruction comes on the lion in spite of his strength (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.6">Psa 58:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>). Five different Hebrew terms here occur for "lion." The raging of the lion (the tearer), and the roaring of the bellowing lion and the teeth of the young lions, not whelps, but grown up enough to hunt for prey. The strong lion, the whelps of the lioness (not the stout lion, as in English Version) [Barnes and Umbreit]. The various phases of wickedness are expressed by this variety of terms: obliquely, Job, his wife, and children, may be hinted at by the lion, lioness, and whelps. The one verb, "are broken," does not suit both subjects; therefore, supply "the roaring of the bellowing lion is silenced." The strong lion dies of want at last, and the whelps, torn from the mother, are scattered, and the race becomes extinct. <div eID="gen6544" type="x-p"/>
entries.9adbd82b05ad036baee33d7f5a6ddb248f35117d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4521"/><div sID="gen6545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4521"/><hi type="bold">12. a thing--</hi>Hebrew, a "word." Eliphaz confirms his view by a divine declaration which was secretly and unexpectedly imparted to him.<div eID="gen6545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a little--</hi>literally, "a whisper"; implying the still silence around, and that more was conveyed than articulate words could utter (<reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">2Co 12:4</reference>). <div eID="gen6546" type="x-p"/>
entries.20acac5232f14a5981ab846593ec27a5c0be11fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4522"/><div sID="gen6547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4522"/><hi type="bold">13. In thoughts from the visions of the night--</hi>[So Winer]. While revolving night visions previously made to him (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.29">Da 2:29</reference>). Rather, "In my manifold (Hebrew, divided) thoughts, before the visions of the night commenced"; therefore not a delusive dream (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>) [Umbreit].<div eID="gen6547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deep sleep--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.2.21">Ge 2:21</reference>; 15:12). <div eID="gen6548" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e19a24920ee7a88254788bccc7d8cd584ce5b0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4523"/><div sID="gen6549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4523"/><hi type="bold">16. It stood still--</hi>At first the apparition glides before Eliphaz, then stands still, but with that shadowy indistinctness of form which creates such an impression of awe; a gentle murmur: not (English Version): there was silence; for in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.12">1Ki 19:12</reference>, the voice, as opposed to the previous storm, denotes a gentle, still murmur. <div eID="gen6549" type="x-p"/>
entries.819b1a8c54dd5b706cd43244da3d23472f753fe1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4524"/><div sID="gen6550" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4524"/><hi type="bold">17. mortal man ... a man--</hi>Two Hebrew words for "man" are used; the first implying his feebleness; the second his strength. Whether feeble or strong, man is not righteous before God.<div eID="gen6550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">more just than God ... more pure than his maker--</hi>But this would be self-evident without an oracle. <div eID="gen6551" type="x-p"/>
entries.645052e86ab317a54324fbd9c507b15e3e8b43f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4525"/><div sID="gen6552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4525"/><hi type="bold">18. folly--</hi>Imperfection is to be attributed to the angels, in comparison with Him. The holiness of some of them had given way (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>), and at best is but the holiness of a creature. Folly is the want of moral consideration [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6552" type="x-p"/>
entries.777977613a33ae1702b8dbae1a2fae006f807c6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4526"/><div sID="gen6553" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4526"/><hi type="bold">19. houses of clay--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>). Houses made of sun-dried clay bricks are common in the East; they are easily washed away (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.27">Mt 7:27</reference>). Man's foundation is this dust (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Ge 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen6553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the moth--</hi>rather, "as before the moth," which devours a garment (<reference osisRef="Job.13.28">Job 13:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.9">Is 50:9</reference>). Man, who cannot, in a physical point of view, stand before the very moth, surely cannot, in a moral, stand before God. <div eID="gen6554" type="x-p"/>
entries.14f97f2f40fc211f6ea216b6a56e81c93c2e6c59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4527"/><div sID="gen6555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4527"/><hi type="bold">20. from morning to evening--</hi>unceasingly; or, better, between the morning and evening of one short day (so <reference osisRef="Exod.18.14">Ex 18:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">Is 38:12</reference>).<div eID="gen6555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They are destroyed--</hi>better, "they would be destroyed," if God withdrew His loving protection. Therefore man must not think to be holy before God, but to draw holiness and all things else from God (<reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>). <div eID="gen6556" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e64ac503dd08e075276a3d3ae4113ac4d682d6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4528"/><div sID="gen6557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4528"/><hi type="bold">21. their excellency--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.4">146:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>). But Umbreit, by an Oriental image from a bow, useless because unstrung: "Their nerve, or string would be torn away." Michaelis, better in accordance with <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>, makes the allusion be to the cords of a tabernacle taken down (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Is 33:20</reference>).<div eID="gen6557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they die, even without wisdom--</hi>rather, "They would perish, yet not according to wisdom," but according to arbitrary choice, if God were not infinitely wise and holy. The design of the spirit is to show that the continued existence of weak man proves the inconceivable wisdom and holiness of God, which alone save man from ruin [Umbreit]. Bengel shows from Scripture that God's holiness (Hebrew, kadosh) comprehends all His excellencies and attributes. De Wette loses the scope, in explaining it, of the shortness of man's life, contrasted with the angels "before they have attained to wisdom." <chapter eID="Job.4"/>

entries.4cde2cf42103a96d7946e0d45d66c72a3e2ce914: <div eID="gen15979" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15980" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15981" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15981" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15980" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15982" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz answers; and accuses Job of impatience, and of despondence in the time of adversity, <reference osisRef="Job.4.1-Job.4.6">Job 4:1-6</reference>; asserts that no innocent man ever perished, and that the wicked are afflicted for their sins, <reference osisRef="Job.4.7-Job.4.11">Job 4:7-11</reference>; relates a vision that he had, <reference osisRef="Job.4.12-Job.4.16">Job 4:12-16</reference>, and what was said to him on the occasion, <reference osisRef="Job.4.17-Job.4.21">Job 4:17-21</reference>. <div eID="gen15982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15983" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15984" type="x-p"/> Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered - For seven days this person and his two friends had observed a profound silence, being awed and confounded at the sight of Job's unprecedented affliction. Having now sufficiently contemplated his afflicted state, and heard his bitter complaint, forgetting that he came as a comforter, and not as a reprover, he loses the feeling of the friend in the haughtiness of the censor, endeavoring to strip him of his only consolation, - the testimony of his conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, he had his conversation among men, - by insinuating that if his ways had been upright, he would not have been abandoned to such distress and affliction; and if his heart possessed that righteousness of which he boasted, he would not have been so suddenly cast down by adversity.
entries.13dd2eee95fe30c820e9956bf05c119eaf1a1d7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15985" type="x-p"/> If we assay to commune with thee - As if he had said, Should I and my friends endeavor to reason with thee ever so mildly, because we shall have many things to say by way of reprehension, thou wilt be grieved and faint; and this we may reasonably infer from the manner in which thou bearest thy present afflictions. Yet as thou hast uttered words which are injurious to thy Maker, who can forbear speaking? It is our duty to rise up on the part of God, though thereby we shall grieve him who is our friend. This was a plausible beginning, and certainly was far from being insincere.
entries.d50b39a629d61025b583f31fc9c016d4e3667c56: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15986" type="x-p"/> Thou hast instructed many - Thou hast seen many in affliction and distress, and thou hast given them such advice as was suitable to their state, and effectual to their relief; and by this means thou hast strengthened the weak hands, and the feeble knees - the desponding have been encouraged, and the irresolute confirmed and excited to prompt and proper actions, by thy counsel and example.
entries.06e4c385ee5140c12784743559917d6414e4b75f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15987" type="x-p"/> But now it is come upon thee - Now it is thy turn to suffer, and give an example of the efficacy of thy own principles; but instead of this, behold, thou faintest. Either, therefore, thou didst pretend to what thou hadst not; or thou art not making a proper use of the principles which thou didst recommend to others.
entries.6118891892f8fd38f62cc9e6115f969723c6beda: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15988" type="x-p"/> Is not this thy fear - I think Coverdale hits the true meaning: Where is now thy feare of God, thy stedfastnesse, thy pacience, and the perfectnesse of thy life? If these be genuine, surely there is no cause for all this complaint, vexation, and despair. That this is the meaning, the next words show.
entries.457bacba78058b7d1c7964a875da5004194fd3f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15989" type="x-p"/> Remember, I pray thee - Recollect, if thou canst, a single instance where God abandoned an innocent man, or suffered him to perish. Didst thou ever hear of a case in which God abandoned a righteous man to destruction? Wert thou a righteous man, and innocent of all hidden crimes, would God abandon thee thus to the malice of Satan? or let loose the plagues of affliction and adversity against thee?
entries.f4f0ab4dbe6b4fabdc4b4d399424709d19ae5529: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15990" type="x-p"/> They that plough iniquity - A proverbial form of speech drawn from nature. Whatever seed a man sows in the ground, he reaps the same kind; for every seed produces its like. Thus Solomon, <reference osisRef="Pro.22.8">Pro 22:8</reference> : "He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity." And St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Gal 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Gal 6:8</reference> : "Be not deceived, God is not mocked; for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh, shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he who soweth to the Spirit, shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting." And of the same nature is that other saying of the apostle, He that soweth sparingly, shall reap sparingly, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.6">2Cor 9:6</reference>. The same figure is employed by the Prophet Hosea <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Hos 8:7</reference> : They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind; and <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">Hos 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.13">Hos 10:13</reference> : Sow to yourselves in righteousness; reap in mercy. Ye have ploughed wickedness; ye have reaped iniquity. The last sentence contains, not only the same image, but almost the same words as those used by Eliphaz. Our Lord expresses the same thing, in the following words: <reference osisRef="Mat.7.16-Mat.7.18">Mat 7:16-18</reference> : Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? Every good tree bringeth forth good fruit, but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. So the Greeks: - Ατης αρουρα θανατον εκκαρπιζεται. <div eID="gen15990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15991" type="x-p"/> Aesch. Ἑπτα επι Θηβαις, ver. 607. "The field of iniquity produces the fruit of death." Ὑβρις γαρ εξανθους εκαρπωσε σταχυν Ατης, ὁθεν παγκλαυτον εξαμᾳ θερος. <div eID="gen15991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15992" type="x-p"/> IB. Περσαι, ver. 823. "For oppression, when it springs, <div eID="gen15992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15993" type="x-p"/> Puts forth the blade of vengeance; and its fruit <div eID="gen15993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15994" type="x-p"/> Yields a ripe harvest of repentant wo." - Potter. <div eID="gen15994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15995" type="x-p"/> The image is common every where because it is a universal law of nature.
entries.1ddf7c9d99dee306d1d428e8d623d8ba73d25a00: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15996" type="x-p"/> By the blast of God they perish - As the noxious and parching east wind blasts and destroys vegetation, so the wicked perish under the indignation of the Almighty.
entries.f2d1d9e86d190cb67996efddeffd02022e4cfd51: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15997" type="x-p"/> The roaring of the lion - By the roaring lion, fierce lion, old lion, stout lion, and lion's whelps, tyrannous rulers of all kinds are intended. The design of Eliphaz in using these figures is to show that even those who are possessed of the greatest authority and power - the kings, rulers, and princes of the earth - when they become wicked and oppressive to their subjects are cast down, broken to pieces, and destroyed, by the incensed justice of the Lord; and their whelps - their children and intended successors, scattered without possessions over the face of the earth.
entries.d00b3d25d9024e5c7ae2b4a5c3052495668fd52d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen15997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15998" type="x-p"/> The old lion perisheth - In this and the preceding verse the word lion occurs five times; and in the original the words are all different: - <div eID="gen15998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15999" type="x-p"/> 1. אריה aryeh, from ארה arah, to tear off. <div eID="gen15999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16000" type="x-p"/> 2. שחל shachal, which as it appears to signify black or dark, may mean the black lion, which is said to be found in Ethiopia and India. <div eID="gen16000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16001" type="x-p"/> 3. כפיר kephir, a young lion, from כפר caphar, to cover, because he is said to hide himself in order to surprise his prey, which the old one does not. <div eID="gen16001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16002" type="x-p"/> 4. ליש lavish, from לש lash, to knead, trample upon; because of his method of seizing his prey. <div eID="gen16002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16003" type="x-p"/> 5. לביא labi, from לבא laba, to suckle with the first milk; a lioness giving suck; at which time they are peculiarly fierce. <div eID="gen16003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16004" type="x-p"/> All these words may point out some quality of the lion; and this was probably the cause why they were originally given: but it is likely that, in process of time, they served only to designate the beast, without any particular reference to any of his properties. We have one and the same idea when we say the lion, the king of beasts, the monarch of the forest, the most noble of quadrupeds, etc.
entries.6d0ed648920f283a25c5787daf3d0a4311cb7111: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16005" type="x-p"/> Now a thing was secretly brought to me - To give himself the more authority, he professes to have received a vision from God, by which he was taught the secret of the Divine dispensations in providence; and a confirmation of the doctrine which he was now stating to Job; and which he applied in a different way to what was designed in the Divine communication. <div eID="gen16005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16006" type="x-p"/> Mine ear received a little thereof - Mr. Good translates, "And mine ear received a whisper along with it." The apparition was the general subject; and the words related <reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>, etc., were the whispers which he heard when the apparition stood still.
entries.28973e61b114b560ab7d0bcdfc8e01105aae8415: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16007" type="x-p"/> From the visions of the night - "It is in vain," says Mr. Good, "to search through ancient or modern poetry for a description that has any pretensions to rival that upon which we are now entering. Midnight-solitude - the deep sleep of all around - the dreadful chill and horripilation or erection of the hair over the whole body - the shivering, not of the muscles only, but of the bones themselves - the gliding approach of the spectre - the abruptness of his pause - his undefined and indescribable form - are all powerful and original characters, which have never been given with equal effect by any other writer." <div eID="gen16007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16008" type="x-p"/> Mr. Hervey's illustration is also striking and natural. "'Twas in the dead of night; all nature lay shrouded in darkness; every creature was buried in sleep. The most profound silence reigned through the universe. In these solemn moments Eliphaz, alone, all wakeful and solitary, was musing on sublime subjects. When, lo! an awful being burst into his apartment. A spirit passed before his face. Astonishment seized the beholder. His bones shivered within him; his flesh trembled all over him; and the hair of his head stood erect with horror. Sudden and unexpected was its appearance; not such its departure. It stood still, to present itself more fully to his view. It made a solemn pause, to prepare his mind for some momentous message. After which a voice was heard. A voice, for the importance of its meaning, worthy to be had in everlasting remembrance. It spoke, and these were its words:"
entries.a0caabbf95a12373c12223b2ea431b08fec778ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16009" type="x-p"/> Shall mortal man - אנוש enosh; Greek βροτος poor, weak, dying man. <div eID="gen16009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16010" type="x-p"/> Be more just than God? - Or, האנוש מאלוה יצדק haenosh meeloah yitsdak; shall poor, weak, sinful man be justified before God? <div eID="gen16010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16011" type="x-p"/> Shall a man - גבר gaber, shall even the strong and mighty man, be pure before his Maker? Is any man, considered merely in and of himself, either holy in his conduct, or pure in his heart? No. He must be justified by the mercy of God, through an atoning sacrifice; he must be sanctified by the Holy Spirit of God, and thus made a partaker of the Divine nature. Then he is justified before God, and pure in the sight of his Maker: and this is a work which God himself alone can do; so the work is not man's work, but God's. It is false to infer, from the words of this spectre, (whether it came from heaven or hell, we know not, for its communication shows and rankles a wound, without providing a cure), that no man can be justified, and that no man can be purified, when God both justifies the ungodly, and sanctifies the unholy. The meaning can be no more than this: no man can make an atonement for his own sins, nor purify his own heart. Hence all boasting is for ever excluded. Of this Eliphaz believed Job to be guilty, as he appeared to talk of his righteousness and purity, as if they had been his own acquisition.
entries.c4584848112de498818f3b9c2fdf33bea35ae198: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16012" type="x-p"/> Behold, he put no trust in his servants - This verse is generally understood to refer to the fall of angels; for there were some of those heavenly beings who kept not their first estate: they did not persevere to the end of their probation, and therefore fell into condemnation, and are reserved in chains of darkness unto the judgment of the great day; <reference osisRef="Jde.1.6">Jde 1:6</reference>. It is said he put no trust in them - he knew that nothing could be absolutely immutable but himself; and that no intelligent beings could subsist in a state of purity, unless continually dependent on himself, and deriving constant supplies of grace, power, and light, from him who gave them their being. <div eID="gen16012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16013" type="x-p"/> And his angels he charged with folly - Not chargeth, as many quote the passage. He charged those with folly who kept not their first estate. It does not appear that he is charging the others in the same way, who continue steadfast. <div eID="gen16013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16014" type="x-p"/> The several translations of this verse, both ancient and modern, are different from each other. Here are the chief: - <div eID="gen16014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16015" type="x-p"/> In angelis suis reperit pravitatem, "In his angels he found perverseness," Vulgate. The Septuagint is nearly the same. II met la lumiere dans ses anges, "He puts light into his angels," French Bible. Even those pure intelligences have continual need of being irradiated by the Almighty; wa-bemalakui neshim temcho, "And he hath put amazement in his angels," Syriac. The Arabic is the same. In angelis suis ponet gloriationem, "In his angels he will put exultation," Montanus. The Hebrew is תהלה toholah, irradiation, from הלה halah, to irradiate, glister, or shine. In this place we may consider angels (מלאכים malachim) as heavenly or earthly messengers or angels of the Lord; and the glory, influence, and honor of their office as being put in them by the Most High. They are as planets which shine with a borrowed light. They have nothing but what they have received. Coverdale translates the whole verse thus: Beholde he hath founde unfaythfulnesse amonge his owne servaunts and proude disobedience amonge his angels. The sense is among all these interpreters; and if the fallen angels are meant, the passage is plain enough.
entries.5269200d3686c485781c13ec6ee39537019e1c85: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16016" type="x-p"/> How much less - Rather, with the Vulgate, How much more? If angels may be unstable, how can man arrogate stability to himself who dwells in an earthly tabernacle, and who must shortly return to dust? Crushed before the moth? The slightest accident oftentimes destroys. "A fly, a grape-stone, or a hair can kill." Great men have fallen by all these. This is the general idea in the text, and it is useless to sift for meanings.
entries.fdbb614131578eaeb758556c2102cfe859d8f401: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16017" type="x-p"/> They are destroyed from morning to evening - In almost every moment of time some human being comes into the world, and some one departs from it. Thus are they "destroyed from morning to evening." <div eID="gen16017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16018" type="x-p"/> They perish for ever - יאבדו yobedu; peribunt, they pass by; they go out of sight; they moulder with the dust, and are soon forgotten. Who regards the past generation now among the dead? Isaiah has a similar thought, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa 57:1</reference> : "The righteous perisheth, and No Man Layeth It to Heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come." Some think that Isaiah borrowed from Job; this will appear possible when it has been proved, which has never yet been done, that the writer of this book flourished before Isaiah. If, however, he borrowed the above thought, it must be allowed that it has been wondrously improved by coming through his hands.
entries.fe2e0a002a0946c4d2df6ee989147dee5a7f1d88: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16019" type="x-p"/> Doth not their excellency - go away! - Personal beauty, corporeal strength, powerful eloquence, and various mental endowments, pass away, or are plucked up by the roots; they are no more seen or heard among men, and their memory soon perisheth. <div eID="gen16019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16020" type="x-p"/> They die, even without wisdom - If wisdom means the pursuit of the best end, by the most legitimate and appropriate means, the great mass of mankind appear to perish without it. But, if we consider the subject more closely, we shall find that all men die in a state of comparative ignorance. With all our boasted science and arts, how little do we know! Do we know any thing to perfection that belongs either to the material or spiritual world? Do we understand even what matter is? What is its essence? Do we understand what spirit is? Then, what is its essence? Almost all the phenomena of nature, its grandest operations, and the laws of the heavenly bodies, have been explained on the principle of gravitation or attraction; but in what does this consist? Who can answer? We can traverse every part of the huge and trackless ocean by means of the compass; but who understands the nature of magnetism on which all this depends? We eat and drink in order to maintain life; but what is nutrition, and how is it effected? This has never been explained. Life depends on respiration for its continuance; but by what kind of action is it, that in a moment the lungs separate the oxygen, which is friendly to life, from the nitrogen, which would destroy it; suddenly absorbing the one, and expelling the other? Who, among the generation of hypothesis-framers, has guessed this out? Life is continued by the circulation of the blood; but by what power and law does it circulate? Have the systole and diastole of the heart, on which this circulation depends, ever been satisfactorily explained? Most certainly not. Alas, we die without wisdom; and must die, to know these, and ten thousand other matters equally unknown, and equally important. To be safe, in reference to eternity, we must know the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom he has sent; whom to know is life eternal. This knowledge, obtained and retained, will entitle us to all the rest in the eternal world.  <chapter eID="Job.4"/> <div eID="gen16020" type="x-p"/>

entries.a28d77d073dc26448c8532c235f53138d3aee38a: <reference osisRef="Job.4.1">Job 4:1</reference> <div eID="gen6975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6976" type="x-p"/> In reply to Sommer, who in his excellent <hi type="italic">biblische Abhandlungen</hi>, 1846, considers the octastich as the extreme limit of the compass of the strophe, it is sufficient to refer to the Syriac strophe-system. It is, however, certainly an impossibility that, as Ewald (<hi type="italic">Jahrb</hi>. ix. 37) remarks with reference to the first speech of Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Job.38.39">Job 38-39</reference>, the strophes can sometimes extend to a length of 12 lines = Masoretic verses, consequently consist of 24 στίχοι and more. Then Eliphaz the Temanite began, and said:
entries.0b41d36f32fc761e37844e8d99d2aad39118999d: <reference osisRef="Job.4.2-Job.5.2">Job 4:2-5   2</reference>  If one attempts a word with thee, will it grieve thee? <div eID="gen6976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6977" type="x-p"/> And still to restrain himself from words, who is able?   3  Behold, thou hast instructed many, <div eID="gen6977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6978" type="x-p"/> And the weak hands thou hast strengthened.   4  The stumbling turned to thy words, <div eID="gen6978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6979" type="x-p"/> And the sinking knees thou hast strengthened.   5  But now it cometh to thee, thou art grieved; <div eID="gen6979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6980" type="x-p"/> Now it toucheth thee, thou despondest. <div eID="gen6980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6981" type="x-p"/> The question with which Eliphaz beings, is certainly one of those in which the tone of interrogation falls on the second of the paratactically connected sentences: Wilt thou, if we speak to thee, feel it unbearable? Similar examples are <reference osisRef="Job.4.21">Job 4:21</reference>; Num 16:22; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jer 8:4</reference>; and with interrogative Wherefore? <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference> : comp. the similar paratactic union of sentences, <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">Job 2:10</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.3.11">Job 3:11</reference></hi>. The question arises here, whether נסּה is an Aramaic form of writing for נשּׂא (as the <hi type="italic">Masora</hi> in distinction from <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference> takes it), and also either future, Wilt thou, if we raise, i.e., utter, etc.; or passive, as Ewald formerly,<note placement="foot">In the second edition, comp. <hi type="italic">Jahrb</hi>. ix. 37, he explains it otherwise: “If we attempt a word with thee, will it be grievous to thee <hi type="italic">quod aegre feras</hi>?” But that, however, must be נסּה; the form נסּה can only be <hi type="italic">third pers</hi>. Piel: If any one attempts, etc., which, according to Ewald’s construction, gives no suitable rendering.</note> <div eID="gen6981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6982" type="x-p"/> If a word is raised, i.e., uttered, דּבר נשׂא, like משׁל נשׂא, <reference osisRef="Job.27.1">Job 27:1</reference>; or whether it is <hi type="italic">third pers. Piel,</hi> with the signification, attempt, <hi type="italic">tentare</hi>, Ecc 7:23. The last is to be preferred, because more admissible and also more expressive. נסּה followed by the <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> is a hypothetic <hi type="italic">praet.,</hi> Supposing that, etc., wilt thou, etc., as e.g., Job 23:10. מלּין is the Aramaic <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. of מלּה, which is more frequent in the book of Job than the Hebrew <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. מלּים. The <hi type="italic">futt.,</hi> Job 4:3., because following the <hi type="italic">perf.,</hi> are like <hi type="italic">imperfects</hi> in the western languages: the expression is like Isa 35:3. In עתּה כּי, <reference osisRef="Job.4.5">Job 4:5</reference>, כּי has a temporal signification, Now when, Ges. §155, 1, <hi type="italic">e</hi>, (<hi type="italic">b</hi>).
