entries.791c82712c5e017baf6ecb3fb636e6e3f9f99f6f: Job 4:6-11   6  Is not thy piety thy confidence, <div eID="gen6982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6983" type="x-p"/> Thy Hope? And the uprightness of thy ways?   7  Think now: who ever perished, being innocent?! <div eID="gen6983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6984" type="x-p"/> And where have the righteous been cut off?!   8  As often as I saw, those who ploughed evil <div eID="gen6984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6985" type="x-p"/> And sowed sorrow, - they reaped the same.   9  By the breath of Eloah they perished, <div eID="gen6985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6986" type="x-p"/> By the breath of His anger they vanished away. 10  The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the shachal, <div eID="gen6986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6987" type="x-p"/> And the teeth of the young lions, are rooted out. 11  The lion wanders about for want of prey, <div eID="gen6987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6988" type="x-p"/> And the lioness’ whelps are scattered. <div eID="gen6988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6989" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.4.6">Job 4:6</reference> all recent expositors take the last <hi type="italic">waw</hi> as <hi type="italic">waw apodosis:</hi> And thy hope, is not even this the integrity of thy way? According to our punctuation, there is no occasion for supposing such an application of the <hi type="italic">waw apodosis,</hi> which is an error in a clause consisting only of substantives, and is not supported by the examples, <reference osisRef="Job.15.17">Job 15:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job 23:12</reference>; 2Sa 22:41.<note placement="foot">We will not, however, dispute the possibility, for at least in Arabic one can say, <hi type="italic">zı̂d f - hkı̂m</hi> Zeid, he is wise. Grammarians remark that Arab. <hi type="italic">zı̂d</hi> in this instance is like a hypothetical sentence: If any one asks, etc. <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.34">2Sa 15:34</reference> is similar.</note> תקותך is the permutative of the ambiguous כסלתך, which, from כּסל, to be fat, signifies both the awkwardness of stupidity and the boldness of confidence. The addition of הוּא to מי, <reference osisRef="Job.4.7">Job 4:7</reference>, like <reference osisRef="Job.13.19">Job 13:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.3">Job 17:3</reference>, makes the question more earnest: <hi type="italic">quis tandem,</hi> like זה מי, <hi type="italic">quisnam</hi> (Ges. §122, 2). In <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>, כּאשׁר is not comparative, but temporal, and yet so that it unites, as usual, what stands in close connection with, and follows directly upon, the preceding: When, so as, as often as I had seen those who planned and worked out evil (comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pro 22:8</reference>), I also saw that they reaped it. That the ungodly, and they alone, perish, is shown in Job 4:10. under the simile of the lions. The Hebrew, like the oriental languages in general, is rich in names for lions; the reason of which is, that the lion-tribe, although now become rarer in Asia, and of which only a solitary one is found here and there in the valley of the Nile, was more numerous in the early times, and spread over a wider area.<note placement="foot">Vid., Schmarda, <hi type="italic">Geographische Verbreitung der Thiere</hi>, i. 210, where, among other things, we read: The lion in Asia is driven back at almost all points, and also in Africa has been greatly diminished; for hundreds of lions and panthers were used in the Roman amphitheatres, whilst at the present time it would be impossible to procure so large a number.</note> שׁחל, which the old expositors often understood as the panther, is perhaps the maneless lion, which is still found on the lower Euphrates and Tigris. נתע = נתץ, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.7">Psa 58:7</reference>, <hi type="italic">evellere, elidere,</hi> by zeugma, applies to the voice also. All recent expositors translate <reference osisRef="Job.4.11">Job 4:11</reference> <hi type="italic">init.</hi> wrongly: the lion perishes. The participle אבד is a stereotype expression for wandering about viewless and helpless (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deu 26:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Isa 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.176">Psa 119:176</reference>, and freq.). The <hi type="italic">part.,</hi> otherwise remarkable here, has its origin in this usage of the language. The parallelism is like Psa 92:10.
entries.9934af89373b9cb849306602e720f414c4e7be69: Job 4:12-16 12  And a word reached me stealthily, <div eID="gen6989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6990" type="x-p"/> And my ear heard a whisper thereof. 13  In the play of thought, in visions of the night, <div eID="gen6990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6991" type="x-p"/> When deep sleep falleth on men, 14  Fear came upon me, and trembling; <div eID="gen6991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6992" type="x-p"/> And it caused the multitude of my bones to quake with fear. 15  And a breathing passed over my face; 16  It stood there, and I discerned not its appearance: <div eID="gen6992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6993" type="x-p"/> An image was before my eyes; <div eID="gen6993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6994" type="x-p"/> A gentle murmur, and I heard a voice. <div eID="gen6994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6995" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> יגגּב, like Jdg 2:1; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">Psa 80:9</reference>, is ruled by the following <hi type="italic">fut. consec.:</hi> <hi type="italic">ad me furtim delatum est</hi> (not <hi type="italic">deferebatur</hi>). Eliphaz does not say אלי ויגנּב (although he means a single occurrence), because he desires, with pathos, to put himself prominent. That the word came to him so secretly, and that he heard only as it were a whisper (שׁמץ, according to Arnheim, in distinction from שׁמע, denotes a faint, indistinct impression on the ear), is designed to show the value of such a solemn communication, and to arouse curiosity. Instead of the prosaic ממּנוּ, we find here the poetic pausal-form מנהוּ expanded from מנּוּ, after the form מנּי, <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference>; Psa 18:23. מן is partitive: I heard only a whisper, murmur; the word was too sacred and holy to come loudly and directly to his ear. It happened, as he lay in the deep sleep of night, in the midst of the confusion of thought resulting from nightly dreams. שׂעפּים (from שׂעיף, branched) are thoughts proceeding like branches from the heart as their root, and intertwining themselves; the מן which follows refers to the cause: there were all manner of dreams which occasioned the thoughts, and to which they referred (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.33.15">Job 33:15</reference>); תּרדּמה, in distinction from שׁנה, sleep, and תּנוּמה, slumber, is the deep sleep related to death and ecstasy, in which man sinks back from outward life into the remotest ground of his inner life. In <reference osisRef="Job.4.14">Job 4:14</reference>, קראני, from קרא = קרה, to meet (Ges. §75, 22), is equivalent to קרני (not קרני, as Hirz., first edition, wrongly points it; comp. <reference osisRef="Gen.44.29">Gen 44:29</reference>). The subject of הפחיד is the undiscerned ghostlike something. Eliphaz was stretched upon his bed when רוּח, a breath of wind, passed (חלף( dessap, similar to <reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Isa 21:1</reference>) over his face. The wind is the element by means of which the spirit-existence is made manifest; comp. 1Ki 19:12, where Jehovah appears in a gentle whispering of the wind, and <reference osisRef="Acts.2.2">Act 2:2</reference>, where the descent of the Holy Spirit is made known by a mighty rushing. רוּח, πνεῦμα, Sanscrit <hi type="italic">âtma</hi>, signifies both the immaterial spirit and the air, which is proportionately the most immaterial of material things.<note placement="foot">On wind and spirit, vid., Windischmann, <hi type="italic">Die Philosophie im Fortgang der Weltgesch</hi>. S. 1331ff.</note> <div eID="gen6995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6996" type="x-p"/> His hair bristled up, even every hair of his body; סמּר, not causative, but intensive of <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>. יעמד has also the ghostlike appearance as subject. Eliphaz could not discern its outline, only a תמוּנה, <hi type="italic">imago quaedam</hi> (the most ethereal word for form, Num 12:8; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>, of μορφή or δόξα of God), was before his eyes, and he heard, as it were proceeding from it, רקל דּממה, i.e., <hi type="italic">per hendiadyn:</hi> a voice, which spoke to him in a gentle, whispering tone, as follows:
entries.02e2402c9809ce0cd7e948fb53a6b2ee8da92d10: Job 4:17-21 17  Is a mortal just before Eloah, <div eID="gen6996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6997" type="x-p"/> Or a man pure before his Maker? 18  Behold, He trusteth not His servants! <div eID="gen6997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6998" type="x-p"/> And His angels He chargeth with imperfection. 19  How much more those who dwell in houses of clay, <div eID="gen6998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6999" type="x-p"/> They are crushed as though they were moths. 20  From morning until evening, - so are they broken in pieces: <div eID="gen6999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7000" type="x-p"/> Unobserved they perish for ever. 21  Is it not so: the cord of their tent in them is torn away, <div eID="gen7000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7001" type="x-p"/> So they die, and not in wisdom? <div eID="gen7001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7002" type="x-p"/> The question arises whether מן is comparative: <hi type="italic">prae Deo,</hi> on which Mercier with penetration remarks: <hi type="italic">justior sit oportet qui immerito affligitur quam qui immerito affligit;</hi> or causal: <hi type="italic">a Deo, h.e., ita ut a Deo justificetur.</hi> All modern expositors rightly decide on the latter. Hahn justly maintains that עם and בּעיני are found in a similar connection in other places; and <reference osisRef="Job.32.2">Job 32:2</reference> is perhaps not to be explained in any other way, at least that does not restrict the present passage. By the servants of God, none but the angels, mentioned in the following line of the verse, are intended. שׂים with בּ signifies <hi type="italic">imputare</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.15">1Sa 22:15</reference>); in <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.1.22">Job 1:22</reference>) we read תּפלה, <hi type="italic">absurditatem</hi> (which Hupf. wishes to restore even here), joined with the verb in this signification. The form תּהלה is certainly not to be taken as <hi type="italic">stultitia</hi> from the verb הלל; the half vowel, and still less the absence of the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, will not allow this. תּרן (Olsh. §213, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), itself uncertain in its etymology, presents no available analogy. The form points to <hi type="italic">a Lamedh-He</hi> verb, as תּרמה from רמה, so perhaps from הלה, <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נהלא, <hi type="italic">remotus</hi>, Mic 4:7 : being distant, being behind the perfect, difference; or even from הלה (Targ. הלא, <hi type="italic">Pa</hi>. הלּי) = לאה, weakness, want of strength.<note placement="foot">Schnurrer compares the Arabic <hi type="italic">wahila</hi>, which signifies to be relaxed, forgetful, to err, to neglect. Ewald, considering the ת as radical, compares the Arabic <hi type="italic">dll</hi>, to err, and <hi type="italic">tâl</hi>, <hi type="italic">med</hi>. <hi type="italic">wau</hi>, to be dizzy, unconscious; but neither from והל nor from תּהל can the substantival form be sustained.</note> <div eID="gen7002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7003" type="x-p"/> Both significations will do, for it is not meant that the good spirits positively sin, as if sin were a natural necessary consequence of their creatureship and finite existence, but that even the holiness of the good spirits is never equal to the absolute holiness of God, and that this deficiency is still greater in spirit-corporeal man, who has earthiness as the basis of his original nature. At the same time, it is presupposed that the distance between God and created earth is disproportionately greater than between God and created spirit, since matter is destined to be exalted to the nature of the spirit, but also brings the spirit into the danger of being degraded to its own level.

What in them was a Vice, in thee, it seems, is become a Virtue.                   <ns0:p n="6">6. Is not this thy Fear, thy Confidence, the Up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rightness of thy Ways, and thy Hope? <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">So the sense is, We now plainly see what was the nature and Complexion of <ns0:hi>thy Fear</ns0:hi> of God, <ns0:hi>thy Confidence</ns0:hi> in him, <ns0:hi>the Upright<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of thy Ways, and thy Hope</ns0:hi> in Gods Mercy, which thou didst make shew and boast of, and for which thou wast become so famous. Thy present carriage discovereth to thy self and others, that it was but meer Talk and appearance, and there was nothing sound and sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cere in it. In thy prosperity it was easie to make a splendid pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession of Religion; but men are best known by Affliction, and this now sheweth of what metal thou art made: For now thou dost cast off thy Fear of God, and all thy Confidence and Hope in him, and hast let go that Integrity of thy ways, which hitherto thou didst seem to hold fast; whereas true Piety is uniform, and constant, and stedfast in all varieties of conditions, and under all Trials and Temptations. But this Translation removes the <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> from its proper place, and changeth the Order of the words, which is this in the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>thy Hope, and the Uprightness of thy ways,</ns0:hi> which words may be restored to their own Order, and with that variation our Tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slation may stand, and this seems to be the true sense. And so here are four distinct Questions, <ns0:hi>Is not this thy Fear? Is not this thy Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fidence? Is not this thy Hope? Is not this the Uprightness of thy ways?</ns0:hi> But others make only two Questions, and render the words either thus; Is <ns0:hi>not</ns0:hi> (or rather, Was <ns0:hi>not) thy Fear</ns0:hi> (of God) <ns0:hi>thy Confidence? And the Uprightness of thy Ways thy Hope? i. e.</ns0:hi> Did not thy <ns0:hi>Fear</ns0:hi> of God, and <ns0:hi>the Integrity of thy Life,</ns0:hi> of which thou didst make such eminent Profession, proceed only from the love of thy self, and of this present World? And from <ns0:hi>thy Confidence and Hope</ns0:hi> that God would bless and prosper thee for it? For now when God with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />draws his Favour and Blessings from thee, thy Religion is vanished, and thou hast cast off all Fear and Reverence of God, as thy impi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous Speeches shew. Or thus: Would <ns0:hi>not thy Fiar be thy Confidence, and the Uprightness of thy Ways thy Hope? i. e.</ns0:hi> If thou hadst indeed that <ns0:hi>Fear</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Integrity</ns0:hi> to which thou pretendest, it would give thee good ground of <ns0:hi>Hope and Confidence</ns0:hi> in the midst of all thy distresses, and thou wouldst not so faint and sink under thy Calamities, as now thou dost, for want of a solid foundation of true Prety. But both these Translations, besides other Inconveniences, stumble at the same stone, and pervert the Order of the Words in the Hebrew Text, of which see before; which is not to be allowed without some kind of necessity, which is not in this case.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. Remember, I pray thee, <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Give me one Example hereof out of all thy Experience or Reading.</ns0:note> who <ns0:hi>ever</ns0:hi> perished, <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Was so utterly undone, as thou art, so miserably afflicted by such unparallel'd and various Judgments from God and Men, all conspiring against thee.</ns0:note> being innocent? <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Who had not by his wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness provoked so merciful a God to do that which is so unusual, and in some sort unpleasing to himself. Therefore thou art guilty of some great, though secret, Crimes, and thy Sin hath now found thee out, and hath brought down these stupendious Plagues upon thee.</ns0:note> or where were the righteous cut off? <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By the Sicle of Divine Vengeance before his time, which is like to be thy case. His Judgment herein was rash and false, but not without some appearance of Truth: For God had made many Promises, not only of spiritual and eternal, but also of temporal Blessings, to all that should faithfully serve and obey him, which accordingly he did from time to time confer upon them, as we see by the Examples of <ns0:hi>Noah, Lot, Abraham, Isaac,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Jacob,</ns0:hi> and doubtless many others which had lived in or before their days. And this was Gods usual method under all the times of the Old Testament, as we see by the People of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> who were generally either in an happy and flou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rishing<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or in an afflicted and miserable State, according to their Obedience to God, or their Apostacy from him. And therefore it is not strange that they fell into this mistake: But allowing for this mistake, and the consequence of it, his uncharitable Opinion of <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> the method which he useth with <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> is commendable, and to be imitated by others in their dealing with persons in Sickness or Affliction: For he doth not flatter him in his Sins, nor immediately and unseasonably apply Comforts to him; but endeavours to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vince him of his Sins, and to bring him to Repentance, as the only regular way to his Remedy.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Shall mortal Man be more just than God? <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Sense is, Thou O <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> dost presumptuously accuse God for dealing harshly and unrighteously with thee, in sending thee in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the World upon such hard terms, and punishing an innocent and righteous man with such unparallel'd severity; but consider things calmly within thy self, If God and thou come to a Trial be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore any equal Judge, canst thou think that thou wiltst go away ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stified, and the great God shall be condemned. No righteous man will punish another without cause, or more than he deserves; and therefore if God do so with thee, as thy words imply, he is less just than a man: which is blasphemous and absurd to imagine.</ns0:note> shall a man <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">A great and mighty man, as this word signifies, a man eminent for Wisdom, or Justice, or Power, or any other perfections, such as thou art thought by thy self or others to be; who therefore might expect more favour than a poor miserable and contemptible man, which the word, <ns0:hi>enosch,</ns0:hi> used in the former Branch, signifies. So he an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticipates this Objection which <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> might make.</ns0:note> be more pure than his Maker? <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">An unanswera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Argument against <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> He made thee, and that for himself and his own Glory, and therefore hath an unquestionable right to deal with thee, and dispose of thee, the work of his Hands, as he sees fit. <ns0:hi>Wo to him that striveth with his maker,</ns0:hi> Isa. 45. 9. Besides he made man just and pure, if any man have any thing of Justice or Purity in him, it is derived from God the undoubted and only Fountain of it, and therefore it must necessarily be in God in a far more e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minent degree.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. Behold, <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This deserves thy serious consideration. These and the follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing words seem to be the words of <ns0:hi>Eliphaz,</ns0:hi> explaining the former Vision, and applying it to <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s Case, and enforcing it by further Arguments.</ns0:note> he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15. 15. and 25. 4. 2 Pet. 2. 4.</ns0:note> put no trust in his Servants <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In his Angels, as appears both by the next words of this Verse, where they are called by way of Explication and Restriction, <ns0:hi>his Angels;</ns0:hi> and by the next Verse where men are opposed to them. They are called <ns0:hi>his Servants</ns0:hi> by way of Emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nency, that general name being here appropriated to the chief of the kind, as is very usual in all Authors in like cases; and withal to intimate that Soveraign Dominion which the great God hath over the glorious Angels, and much more over men, by vertue whereof he hath an unquestionable Authority to treat them ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to his good Pleasure. And these God is said to <ns0:hi>put no trust in,</ns0:hi> because he could not be confident that they, if left to them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, and destitute of the succours of his Power and Grace, would continue to be loyal, and faithful, and serviceable to him, and would not revolt from him, as some of their Brethren had done. And for this cause God was pleased, after some time of Trial, to give some special and further Grace, either by Christ or otherwise, whereby they should be infallibly confirmed in the State of Grace & Felicity.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>not in his Angels,</ns0:hi> in whom <ns0:hi>he put light.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> and his Angels he charged with Folly: <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>with Vanity: i. e.</ns0:hi> He discerned Folly and Vanity in the Angelical Natures, when he had first made them; which although he saw and pronounced them, no less than the visible Creatures, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to be <ns0:hi>very good</ns0:hi> in themselves, & free from the least degree or tincture of sin; yet comparing them with himself, and considering them in themselves alone, he saw something of Folly and Vanity in their ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry Natures, because they were Creatures, and therefore Subject to manifold changes, and, among others, to fall from God, or into sin; as it appeared by the sad experience of some of them. Seeing therefore the Angels, which so far exceed Mankind in Wisdom, and Strength, and Purity, and Justice, and all other perfections, do fall incomparably short of God in these things, it is most absurd as well as impious, to think that Man is more just or pure than God, as was said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17. and as thou, O <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> seemest to surmise. Others, Nor (Heb. <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> not; the negative Particle being repeated out of the former Branch of the Verse, as it is <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 9. 18. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 26. and elsewhere,) <ns0:hi>in his Angels,</ns0:hi> in whom (both which particles are frequently understood, as hath been proved before) <ns0:hi>he put Light,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>splendor,</ns0:hi> to wit, singular Wisdom, and Purity, beyond what he put in Man.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:p n="19">19. How much less <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Understand, <ns0:hi>doth he put trust</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> &c.                      <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> are crushed <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>they crush them, i. e.</ns0:hi> they are or will be crushed.                         <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Sooner than a Moth is crushed, which is easily done by a Gentle touch of the Fingers. An Hyper<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bolical Expression.
